study.title: Mechanical methods vs NSAIDs for discogenic low back pain
study.evidence_note: Single randomised trial; no effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
study.confidence_note: Methods and key results were stated clearly, but reporting was sparse for attrition, blinding, and effect estimates.
study.impact_line: Short-term pain and mobility improved in all groups; MIT looked best, but the report gives no effect sizes or CIs.
summary: 4 groups of 70 patients each were compared: Saunders traction, McKenzie, MIT, and ketoprofen.
All groups improved after treatment and at follow-up, but the paper reports no mean differences or CIs.
MIT was reported as best on VAS and Schober; McKenzie was best on Laitinen.
Randomisation and concealed allocation were reported, but outcome assessment was self-reported and unblinded.

pico.p: Adults aged 30–60 years with chronic discogenic low back pain
pico.i: Multiple impulse therapy, McKenzie method, or Saunders lumbar traction
pico.c: Ketoprofen pharmacotherapy; also active method-to-method comparisons
pico.o: Pain on Laitinen and VAS, and mobility on the Schober test

limits: No effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported for the main comparisons.
Pain was self-reported, and participants knew their treatment.
No attrition details or protocol were reported.
All patients also received Sollux lamp treatment.
study.bottom_line: All four groups improved short term. MIT was favoured on VAS and Schober, while McKenzie led Laitinen. With no effect sizes or CIs, this is hypothesis-generating, not a basis to choose one treatment.

methods.setting: Motor Rehabilitation Center in Piotrkow Trybunalski, Poland
methods.participants: 280 patients aged 30–60 years with chronic discogenic low back pain confirmed by imaging
methods.intervention: Saunders traction, McKenzie method, multiple impulse therapy, or ketoprofen
methods.comparator: Active treatment groups plus pharmacotherapy comparator
methods.primary_outcome: Subjective pain on Laitinen and VAS; Schober test for mobility

results.result: McKenzie was reported as best; Saunders was similarly effective
results.detail: The paper states that McKenzie produced the best Laitinen results and that Saunders was similarly effective, but it does not report the underlying values.
ANOVA after treatment and Welch testing at 30 days found MIT differed from the other groups; all groups also improved within group.

results.result: MIT was best vs McKenzie and drugs
results.detail: The paper reports MIT had slightly but significantly better Schober results than McKenzie, and better results than drug treatment, with greater flexion at 30 days.

how_to_apply: Treat the finding as short-term comparative information, not proof that MIT is superior.
Expect all groups to improve over treatment and follow-up.
Do not use the paper alone to choose MIT over McKenzie or traction.
Remember every group also received blue-filter Sollux lamp treatment.
Use the result as a hypothesis-generating study for discogenic low back pain.
applies_to: Adults 30–60 years with imaging-confirmed discogenic low back pain
Short-term supervised rehabilitation in a clinic setting

strengths: Four groups were equal in size.
Baseline age and sex balance looked similar.
weaknesses: No effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
Co-intervention with Sollux lamp across all groups.
appraisal.funding_conflicts: No external funding; authors declared no conflicts of interest.

grade.reason: Self-reported outcomes were measured in an unblinded trial, with no attrition reporting or protocol.
Adults with imaging-confirmed discogenic low back pain match the condition of interest.
No effect sizes or 95% CIs were reported, so precision cannot be judged.

clinical_significance: No MCID or smallest worthwhile change can be applied because the paper does not report the mean changes or confidence intervals.
The report says MIT was best on VAS and Schober, but the size of benefit is unknown.
The result could be clinically important, trivial, or uncertain; the paper does not let us distinguish that.
comparator_fairness: The comparators were credible active treatments, not a pure wait-list.
Dose and contact time were not matched across groups.
The ketoprofen arm had less therapist contact than the physical treatment arms.
All groups also received Sollux lamp treatment, which blurs the contrast.
alternative_explanations: Natural recovery may explain part of the improvement.
Regression to the mean may have contributed.
Expectation and therapist-contact effects could favour the physical methods.
The shared Sollux lamp co-intervention may have influenced all groups.
spin: The conclusion claims MIT is a valuable and safe modality, but the paper does not provide effect sizes or blinded outcome assessment.
Conclusions favour MIT over McKenzie and traction despite mixed outcome leaders and no effect estimates.
fit_with_evidence: Consistent with the 2021 JOSPT low back pain guideline’s support for exercise and manual therapy, but MIT itself remains much less established.
Best read as a small comparative study rather than practice-changing evidence.
external_validity: ✓ Adults with chronic discogenic low back pain
✓ Clinic-based rehabilitation similar to outpatient care
✗ Age limited to 30–60 years and no athletes-specific sample
would_change_my_mind: A larger blinded trial with prespecified outcomes and effect sizes.
A head-to-head study showing MIT clearly beats active physiotherapy on a clinically important outcome.
Longer follow-up showing durable benefit beyond follow-up.

study.patient_explanation: This study compared three physical treatments with an anti-inflammatory medicine for disc-related back pain. All groups improved, but the paper does not give enough numbers to tell how much better one treatment was than another.
open_questions: How much of the improvement came from the shared Sollux lamp?
Would the findings hold beyond follow-up?
Are the between-group differences clinically important?
key_findings: Four equal groups were treated for a short period.
All groups improved on pain and mobility.
MIT was reported as best on VAS and Schober; McKenzie was best on Laitinen.
The study reports randomisation, but not blinding or effect sizes.
